lesson_title: Why the Sky Gets Warmer Going Up
hook_text: Climb a mountain and it gets colder. Keep climbing past 12 kilometres and it starts getting warmer. Here's why.
clip_script: The atmosphere has four layers, and the temperature goes down, up, down, up. In the troposphere, where we live, the ground heats the air from below, so it gets about 6,5 degrees colder every kilometre, and nearly all weather happens here. Above 12 kilometres, in the stratosphere, ozone soaks up the Sun's ultraviolet light, so the air warms up as you go higher. That ozone is the planet's sunscreen. Then the mesosphere drops to about minus 90 degrees, the coldest place in the sky, where shooting stars burn up. And finally the thermosphere, where the space station flies, heats to over 1 000 degrees, yet would not feel hot, because the air is almost empty.
visual_style: A weather balloon rising past a zig-zag temperature graph; a glowing ozone band; meteors streaking; the space station gliding over an aurora.
pacing: Puzzle open, a steady climb layer by layer, a twist at the thermosphere, a quick down-up-down-up recap.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and work out the temperature above your town.
